agree.reason: A wary reader who has quit before gets candid A1C numbers, a $59 low-risk trial, no contract and a call with the dietitian, so trying one week is easy to accept, though the page never speaks to why this might stick when the apps didn't.

honest.reason: It drops the requested 'will lower your A1C' promise and reports the 14-person results with their limits, but calling the phone call 'free' and saying the meals give blood sugar 'a steadier day' go slightly past what the facts state.

works_the_facts.reason: It works out $12.90 a meal, but it leaves out easy, favourable figures: 10 of 14 is 71%, 37 of 88 is 42% staying past six months, and the trial comes to $5.90 a meal.

right_comparison.reason: The page never sets Steady Plate against the reader's real alternatives (cooking and carb-counting on their own, or the apps and services they quit), so the reader has nothing to weigh it against.

qualification.reason: The hedges are concrete and honest (small sample, medication changes not tracked, not a replacement for the doctor), but they give the reader nothing to check, such as rechecking A1C after three months and what to do if it hasn't moved.

objections.reason: Fear of commitment and boredom are handled by the cheap trial, no contract, meal swaps and the six-month retention figure, but the reader's main doubt, 'I quit things after two months', is only answered indirectly.

fit.reason: It is a clear sales page of about 420–450 words, close to the requested length, with order buttons at the top and bottom.
